Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

vignette:
Elena has worked at the city library for forty-two years, a quiet life lived among books and the hushed footsteps of patrons. At seventy-eight, her movements are deliberate, her smile gentle, but her husband, Miguel, sees the tension that has settled deep in her shoulders. He watches her meticulously arranging her small garden, a flurry of constant, restless activity, and knows she is not at peace. The past, which had lain dormant for decades, has returned with a vengeance. It does not arrive as a clear story, but in fragments of sensation and a guilt so profound it feels like a physical weight. She has never been able to put the worst of it into words, not even for him. The memory exists without a narrative, a silent film of terror that plays behind her eyes.

It began sixty years ago, in a damp, earthen cellar beneath a farmhouse. Her family was fleeing, and the soldiers were close. She was eighteen, clutching her six-year-old brother, Javier, trying to muffle his frightened whimpers against her chest. The smell was overwhelming-a mix of wet soil, rotting potatoes, and the sharp, chemical scent of the lye they'd used to clean the floors. When the heavy tread of boots echoed on the floorboards above, Javier began to cry in earnest. Without thinking, moved by sheer panic, Elena clamped her hand over his mouth. She remembers the frantic drumming of his small fists against her arm, the wildness in his eyes as he struggled for air. The boots moved on. The danger passed. But the image of her brother's terrified, suffocated face, and the crushing shame of what she had done, became permanently etched into her being.

In the years that followed, she built a new life in America. She met Miguel, raised two children, and found solace in the orderly silence of the library. But she never escaped the cellar. Now, in her quiet moments, the questions circle endlessly. Why did it have to be us? Why was I the one holding him? What kind of monster smothers a child? She repeatedly scolds herself for that moment of panic, a private, relentless self-flagellation for a sin no one else knows she committed. To keep the thoughts at bay, she throws herself into tasks. At home, it's the garden. At the library, it's endless cataloging and shelving, working with a frantic energy that seems out of place in the calm environment. She stays busy, because in the stillness, the memories find their way in.

Her world has grown smaller over the last few years. She feels a constant, low-level hum of dread, a sense that danger is always imminent. She is watchful, her head snapping up at the sound of the library's heavy oak doors opening, her eyes scanning each new face. Her concentration has frayed; she'll find herself staring at the same line on a page, the words blurring as the scent of damp earth fills her senses, triggered by nothing more than a newly watered potted fern near her desk. When the smell comes, so does the guilt, a hot wave of shame that makes her feel sick to her stomach. She has come to believe that safety exists only within the walls of her own home and in her small corner of the library. She no longer goes to the bustling Sunday market with Miguel or to community gatherings. The unpredictability of the outside world is too much to bear.

The final impetus for seeking help came last month, after the birth of her first great-grandchild. Her granddaughter placed the sleeping baby in her arms. As Elena held the warm, tiny bundle, she was suddenly back in the cellar, the memory of her brother's small, struggling body in her grasp. A cold terror seized her, a fear that she was fundamentally dangerous, capable of terrible harm. She handed the baby back abruptly, her hands trembling. She knew then that she could no longer manage this alone. She wants, more than anything, to be able to hold her great-grandchild without feeling the ghost of that panicked, eighteen-year-old girl who believed she had almost become a monster in a dark, silent cellar sixty years ago.
